confidence_note: From reviews and summaries, not the book text. Old text's bedside scene with an 85-year-old man was dropped as unsourced. The 30-pound child item varies by version and is not used with a number. Whether the book spells out marginal decade exactly as summarised is medium.
facts: Attia contrasts Medicine 2.0, which mainly aims at lifespan and staving off death, with Medicine 3.0.
Medicine 3.0 emphasises prevention, starts from an honest assessment of risk, including the risk of doing nothing, and gives more weight to healthspan.
The marginal decade is the last ten years of life, when people may be alive but unable to do what they enjoy.
Attia wants readers to name what they want to do in that decade and work backward to train for it now; his aim is a bonus decade.
The Centenarian Decathlon: choose ten physical tasks you want to still do late in life, then set today's fitness target backward from them.
Reported sample tasks: getting up from the floor using at most one arm, carrying groceries for several blocks, picking up a child, climbing stairs.
VO2 max falls about 10 percent per decade, faster after 50, so reserve is built in the 40s and 50s.

Items on one version of the list: lifting a twenty-pound suitcase into an overhead compartment, balancing on one leg for thirty seconds, climbing four flights of stairs in three minutes (low; versions differ).
Attia says you need to be quite fit in your 50s to manage picking up a grandchild, hiking or carrying groceries upstairs in your 90s.
scene_details: getting up from the floor with one arm
tension: A long life can end in years without the movements that made it worth living.
